messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a sixty-six-year-old South Asian woman, widowed for several years, who works part-time at a home goods retail store in a mid-sized American city. She presented for psychological assessment following what she described, haltingly, as "something that happened to me that I cannot put away." Her PCL-5 score of 63 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a woman whose inner world has been quietly reorganising itself around a single catastrophic event for months.

Approximately eight months before seeking help, Priya was raped by an acquaintance in the back room of a building she had entered alone with him, trusting that she was safe. The assault took place in a confined space that smelled strongly of cigarette smoke, and it unfolded with a quality of wrongness that she still cannot fully articulate — not only the violation itself but the way he spoke to her afterward, as though nothing had occurred, as though she owed him her composure. She drove herself home. She told no one for weeks.

The memories of that evening do not come to Priya as a narrative. They arrive as a series of still images — what she describes as photographs she cannot stop looking at, each one fixed and overexposed: his face at a particular angle, the texture of the wall she stared at, the arrangement of objects on a shelf. Some moments are searingly clear in this photographic way, while others are simply absent, blank frames where something must have happened but nothing remains. She has come to experience these snapshot memories as a form of ambush, because they arrive not when she chooses to reflect but when her environment reaches into the past and pulls them forward.

Smell is the most reliable trigger. Priya works on the floor of a retail store, and on days when a colleague steps outside to smoke and returns carrying the scent on their clothes, she finds herself suddenly not in the store at all — she is back in that room, looking at one of her photographs. The triggered memory then floods her with a sense of deep injustice, a hot and wordless certainty that something monstrous was done to her and that no one has answered for it. She reported that her employer does not know why, on certain afternoons, she goes very still at the register and has to be spoken to twice.

Being alone with men produces the same cascade. When a male customer lingers near her section or a male manager asks her to stay behind after a shift, the proximity itself functions as a warning, and the warning summons the images. The triggered memories, in turn, confirm what she has come to believe: that the world is not safe, that men cannot be trusted, and that she was foolish to have believed otherwise. This belief has begun to precede the triggers rather than simply follow them — she now scans every male customer who enters the store before he has done anything at all, and that vigilance keeps her nervous system in a state that makes the next trigger more likely to land.

Priya's appraisals of herself and her situation have hardened into something that feels, to her, simply like realism. She is certain she cannot manage even small frustrations — a mislabelled price, a rude customer — without her composure crumbling, and this perceived fragility makes her dread the ordinary provocations of her job. Witnessing even minor social transgressions, someone cutting in line or speaking rudely to a cashier, strikes her as unbearable now, not only because it is unpleasant but because moral violation of any kind pulls her back toward the central one, the one that went unanswered. She had come to believe that nothing in her life held meaning anymore — not her work, not her routines, not the small pleasures that once sustained her as a widow living alone — and this hollowness makes her less equipped to tolerate the daily encounters that trigger her, which in turn deepen her conviction that she is broken beyond repair.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a conversation with her daughter, who noticed that her mother had stopped attending the weekly temple gatherings she had kept for thirty years. Priya came to the first session saying very little about what she wanted, but at the end she said, quietly, that she wanted to know whether what happened to her would be wrong forever, or only for now.
